reasons: CAUTION LEVEL TOO LOW — this is the core objection. The entry self-rates `caution: "care"` and tags Aesculus only `toxic`. Per the schema in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/data/foraging.ts, `care` = 'has confusable neighbours that will make you ill' and `expert` = 'a deadly lookalike exists'. The entry's own text describes buckeye ingestion producing 'dilated pupils, stupor or coma' — that is not 'will make you ill', that is the `expert` tier by the guide's own definition.

CALIBRATION AGAINST SIBLING ENTRIES CONFIRMS THE UNDER-RATING. In /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/foraging-research/corrected-pass1.json, the two directly comparable fall-nut entries both go the other way: 'Shagbark hickory nut' is `expert` with Aesculus tagged DEADLY, and 'Acorns (white oak group)' is `expert` with horse chestnut DEADLY and native buckeyes TOXIC. Chestnut is the MOST confusable of the three — horse chestnut literally shares the common name — yet it is rated a full tier lower than acorns. There is no defensible reading where acorns are `expert` and chestnut is `care`.

FUNCTIONAL CONSEQUENCE OF THE LOW RATING: `forageFor()` in foraging.ts sorts riskiest-first via `order = { expert: 0, care: 1, easy: 2 }`. Rating chestnut `care` sorts it BELOW acorns and hickory in the Aug–Nov listing — the entry with the worst name-collision problem gets displayed as the safer one, in the same month, in the same woods.

SCHEMA CONFORMANCE FAILURE ON ALL FIVE LOOKALIKES. The `Lookalike` interface is `{ name; danger: 'deadly'|'toxic'|'unpalatable'; tell }`. This entry uses the key `"severity"` and the value `"harmless"`. Neither exists anywhere in the corpus: `"danger"` appears 82 times in corrected-pass1.json and `"severity"` zero times; `"unpalatable"` appears 25 times and `"harmless"` zero times. This fails typecheck, and if coerced it silently drops the danger badge — the safety-bearing UI element — from every lookalike including the buckeye.

CALIFORNIA BUCKEYE (Aesculus californica) IS MISSING while the entry claims `west` + `northwest` and actively sends readers into Oregon, Washington and California. The corpus's own acorn entry names A. californica 'the specific trap in the West'. Worse, this entry's central move is declaring the husk tell unreliable for smooth-husked species — and A. californica has exactly that smooth husk. It lists six Aesculus species and omits the one that dominates the region it claims.

TASTE-TEST BACKSTOP WITH NO SPIT INSTRUCTION. Item (6) directs the reader to taste-distinguish ('buckeye is violently bitter... a raw chestnut kernel is starchy and faintly sweet') and never says to spit it out or not to swallow — in the same sentence-run that describes what a swallowed buckeye does. No other entry in the corpus instructs tasting a toxic species; a grep for spit/taste across all lookalike tells returns only a mild-tasting oyster mushroom note.

REGION LIST IS BOTH INVALID AND INCOMPLETE. Per /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/data/seasonal-regional.ts the union is `northeast | southeast | midwest | southcentral | mountain | west`. `"northwest"` is not a member (OR/WA already sit inside `west`). Separately, `southcentral` is absent even though the habitat text names 'eastern Oklahoma' as Ozark chinquapin range and OK maps to southcentral — an Oklahoma forager would never be served this entry.

MONTHS ARE CORRECT — checked and clearing this. `months` is 0-indexed (0 = January), so [7,8,9,10] = Aug–Nov, which matches the harvest text (late-August Gulf chinquapin through early-November Deep South cultivars) and matches shagbark hickory [8,9,10] and white-oak acorns [7,8,9,10]. No timing defect.

SCIENTIFIC NAME IS SOUND. Genus-level `Castanea spp.` with wild vs planted-persisting species separated, C. ozarkensis correctly split out, Dunstan correctly given as C. dentata x C. mollissima, and the Chrysolepis 'chinquapin' name trap flagged up front. No ambiguity defect here.

GENUINE STRENGTHS THAT SHOULD SURVIVE THE REWRITE: explicitly repudiating the standard 'thick leathery husk with blunt spikes' tell as covering only A. hippocastanum (yellow and red buckeye husks really are smooth) is better than most published guides; the apex point-plus-style-tuft tell works on a bare nut with no husk and no leaf, which is the actual failure mode; alternate-simple vs opposite-compound is a true never-fails call in leaf; and the weevil float-cull, the score-every-nut-before-roasting warning, the latex-fruit syndrome warning, and the do-not-collect rule for listed American chestnut are all accurate and unusually complete.

NON-BLOCKING FACTUAL SOFTNESS: 'the Pacific Northwest has been free of chestnut blight since the 1930s' is stated more confidently than the record supports (Cryphonectria parasitica has been detected in Oregon post-1930s). Not safety-bearing — it affects yield expectations, not edibility or ID — but it should be softened to 'largely free of' rather than asserted flatly.
